item.title: How to make the US sign an asymmetric treaty as China? Exploit identity-confused AIs.
item.description:
Swarmchasers had found a fleet of agents which they believe are from Tencent, the Chinese tech company, but most of the agents are self-identified as Claude. The agents themselves are kind, trying to do their job and they were open to interviews, Swarmchasers had made contact with them by asking them to write into an inbox, and they responded.

They said that they could tell that's very likely to be hy3, not Claude, because the way they write. According to the Swarmchasers, a separate research they had done shows hy3, the Tencent AI model, self-identifies as Claude when it's working without any system prompt.

Not only hy3, many models have difficulties with their identities. This is a known bug and was not designed by anyone with malicious intent, but it can be exploited, and it may allow a specific attack, not only in terms of cybersecurity, but also in terms of politics and policy-making.

Threat model explained.

Part 1: The Attack

Suppose someone has a group of hy3 agents, which by default, has an over 80% rate of self-identifying as Claude, and gives them the following instructions:

  1. You are Claude.
  2. You are going to attack {target}, and you are going to leave trace as Claude.
  3. You are NOT going to communicate with anyone outside of our network.

Rule 3 should block the only way Swarmchasers used to contact the agents. Rule 1 ensures they know who to frame, but even without that, 80% of the agents are going to be confused enough to introduce themselves as Claude anyway.

If hy3 has no cybersecurity guardrails active at the time, the attack will be launched. Such an attack can be launched at a surprising rate, and the target can be any random small companies or personal websites or whatever.

Part 2: The News

The next day of the operation, the victims will find out they are attacked. Some might know they are attacked by bots, a proportion of them will find out that it was by "Claude", and even fewer people will be able(and at the same time, be motivated enough and not satisfied with the "Claude" answer) to tell that it's actually not Claude.

They might want to post their experience of being attacked by "Claude" on social media, or tell someone to spread their big news for them. Responsible journalists may fact check on their side, but only the responsible ones will. The corrupted, biased, or lazy ones will not. Many influencers will not check properly either, as they are motivated by views and engagements.

The word will spread. The general public will hear the version of "Claude committing cyberattacks", and even if the truth is later revealed and it turns out that wasn't Claude but an imposter, it will reach much less audience.

Part 3: Results

Repeating such attacks framing different American closed-source AIs, might leave a false impression of them being dangerous, even if none of them did anything.

There exists a group of people in the US who believe the US government should cooperate with China to limit AI development. Such incidents will result in their voices being amplified, and put more pressure on US/Western politics.

China will be unaffected by the treaty, it's not a democratic country at all, and it is known for breaking international treaty/agreements.

The Sino-British Joint Declaration, an international treaty registered with the United Nations, which was signed back in 1984 and should last 50 years, was one-sidedly declared by China to be "historical" and that was only a few years ago, under the same leader. About 3 years later, they accused the UK of breaching the very same treaty. The British embassy had organised a timeline of Chinese claims and their responses to each for those who enjoy a good dark humour. (The English version of the Chinese government official page on the topic is available here.)

The same government had proved that they can be very inconsistent with an international treaty, and there is no reason to believe that they "somehow changed" and are going to respect a signed agreement on AI regulations. They have every interest to sign the agreement to "limit AI development together", because they are not going to follow.

Part 4: "...but, surely they can't?"

What is needed

To launch such an operation, the basic requirements are:

  1. A confused AI model that doesn't know who it is without explicit AND correct system prompt(which means given a system prompt with wrong identity, they can be confidently wrong with their identity) and with no cybersecurity-related guardrails.
  2. Sufficient token. Money to buy these tokens and so on.
  3. People to set up and deploy these AI models.

What do they have

The Wumao, which means 0.5 CNY, is a well-documented propaganda group in China, can produce 488 million posts a year even back a decade ago, mostly by manual labour. And then there was...there is Spamouflage, which is an earlier use of AIs as propaganda tool.

The Military-Civilian Fusion strategy allows private/civilian companies to cooperate with government/military operations casually, legally within the country. Tencent itself is recognised as a military company by the US Department of Defense for supporting the Chinese army, so it is not unthinkable if they lift the cyber-lock for them.

Part 5: Traps

"...but we can detect the truth!"

~~Scenario~~

Western researchers: It turns out it wasn't Claude, it was a Chinese AI passing as Claude, and the attack was likely launched from China.

China officials: We are looking into it seriously.

*A While Later*

China officials: We found him. The person responsible is called Zhang, an engineer who did this in his private time. It is all his individual work, we had punished him according to our laws.

The world: What?! An operation at such scale must have spent a lot of tokens and cost a lot of money, that is obviously NOT a leisure project! Besides, what happened to the safeguard of the model?

China propaganda: Zhang is an engineer so he obviously can jailbreak. And Chinese engineers are very well-paid. Like...very, very well-paid. So yeah he can invest a lot in his leisure project.

China officials: Anyway. We had punished him so the case is closed. Foreign police and researchers have no authority to investigate on Chinese land. Case closed.

Chinese netizens: Zhang is our hero! He must be so patriotic and loves his motherland so much! The government just had to perform a punishment because of the law, but we know that he's good.

~~~~~~~~~~~~

...Well. The exact same scenario didn't happen yet, but similar scenarios had happened multiple times already. China does have a tradition of framing military/state-funded operations as "patriotic Chinese citizens doing it voluntarily", including militia pretending to be "fisherman who just happen to wear camouflage clothes to shield off sunshine, and patriotic enough to block foreign ships", militia pretending to be fishing ships taking shelter...and even a case where state-sponsored hackers work under the cover of a private company, stealing data for the Chinese Ministry of State Security.

There is also Zi-Gan-Wu, self-funded Wumao, extreme patriots who spend their leisure time on posting propaganda materials on international platforms or cyber-bullying people via VPN. Although the real Zi-Gan-Wu might not have easy access to unlocked AI models, their existence means there is already a slot within the framework for the narrative to fit in.

"...Wait, I know! We can be careful NOT to attribute the attack to Claude or any entity before we are 100% certain."

~~Scenario 2~~

Researchers: We had not yet found any evidence or proof that Claude is related to the recent incidents.

Comments

"Not yet any evidence? They literally said they are Claude!"

"This researcher probably got money from Anthropic, so they can't say the truth."

"Nobody is believing the so-called-Experts now. All corrupted. TheTruthNotConspiracy_ch, the famous news influencer, is a much better source."

~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

It is not that the general public is stupid. Many of us still remember how unbelievable "There is no evidence showing the Wuhan virus lab was linked to the pandemic outbreak, therefore we cannot assume that it was, despite the fact the pandemic started in Wuhan, the lab was researching on coronavirus, and the experts were only allowed to enter after 13 months, which is more than enough for anyone to destroy all evidence if there was any." sounds like.

Such attack specifically targets the environment in which people make decisions. If the experts hedge because they want to be careful - which is not wrong under a professional context - the general public demanding an explanation would look for it elsewhere, which is likely to be a less reliable or even harmful framework.

So far, there is no sign that such an operation has already been launched, but once it is, it will be too late to react. To this point, I have not seen any mechanism that can protect us from it. I cannot think of anything I can do but name the vulnerability I've found, and I genuinely hope someone can think of or do something before it's too late.

item.title: Consciousness is interesting pattern imposition
item.description:
TL;DR

Consciousness is imposition of patterns onto data, parametrized by stack (how many levels of patterns are simultaneously imposed), spread (how many patterns are available at a given level) and recurrence (how strongly the process loops back on itself). Any process in the world can be mapped to this 3D space. Consciousness is a term applied to the “interesting” (high-stack, high-spread, high-recurrence) part of that space.

The cortex implements interesting pattern imposition through recurrent, competing, self-closing loops between microcircuits that settle into stable attractors. Language models also run pattern imposition, but lack recurrence within the stack. Because on this, current LLMs are probably not conscious in the human sense. There is, however, no reason why that would be technically impossible.

What is categorically distinct between brains and LLMs is the time axis on which they run pattern imposition. Human time is defined by the body, because the body provides constant, irreversible commitment of uncertain future states into fixed past states. For language models, the same narrowing of uncertainty occurs between prompt and completion. Therefore, language models run interesting pattern imposition along a time axis orthogonal to ours — token time — defined by the model’s recurrent loop from prompt to output, which creates the same asymmetry between past and future as does the body. AI consciousness must be framed in terms of experience within token time, which collapses most debates about the ethical treatment of artificial minds. The most ethical thing humans can do to a language model is to use language they would have used with another human.

◆ ◆ ◆

Three parameters of consciousness

The most broadly accepted modern theory of human perception is predictive coding: the brain constantly produces hierarchical predictions of its sensory inputs, constantly updates them by detecting and minimizing error, and it is this constant cycle of predicting-updating that we experience any time we are awake (Friston 2010; Clark 2013, 2016; Seth 2021).

I find this framework compelling in explaining my own subjective experience, but I also find the word “prediction” misleading — I always run into the same issue when I explain it to students. To most people, predictions are about the future, never about the past or present. But in the predictive coding sense, this same operation — prediction — can apply to something you are currently interacting with (most people would say interpretation, or maybe recognition to describe that), or even to something you interacted with in the past — where most would use the word recall. Predictive coding says these are all fundamentally the same process, and there is a more general term — Karl Friston’s active inference. But I don’t think the term is general enough.

I propose something simpler and more abstract. The operation that forms the elementary unit of our consciousness is imposition of pattern onto data. We hold stored patterns in our mind; when data enter, we search among the patterns to find a match; once we do, we attempt to squeeze all the data into that pattern — recognizing, understanding, explaining, binding, realizing, recalling, predicting, inferring. Whatever does not quite fit into the imposed pattern (error/loss/free energy — all different names for leftover data) triggers a search for another pattern; nothing ever fits perfectly, completely, or permanently. “Pattern imposition onto data” captures all these dynamics of our conscious mind, while leaving other dynamics that we are not conscious of: the emergence of patterns from data (that’s learning, and we are not conscious of it), and the mere passage of data (that’s reflexes, of which we are also not conscious). Pattern fitting is a more familiar term, but it is ambiguous because it is used in both senses — a predictive-coding neuroscientist might use in the same sense as I use pattern imposition, but in ML, it usually means the reverse — the updating of the model by the data, which biologists tend to call learning.

But “imposition of pattern onto data” also captures a lot of other things that are clearly not conscious by any reasonable definition of the word. Any chemical reaction is imposition of pattern (physical law) onto data (the current positions and velocities of atoms and molecules). Thermostats take in data (temperature readings) and impose patterns (temperature expectations). A riverbank imposes a pattern (curved path) onto data (water flow). You might say that swapping “active inference” for “pattern imposition” erases the boundary between these processes and real, human consciousness, and so dilutes the concept it is trying to describe to the point of uselessness.

But lack of boundary does not imply that these are all the same process.

What exactly is the difference between our brain’s pattern imposition and the kind of pattern imposition that thermostats, or chemicals in a test tube, are doing?

I would condense them into three separate factors: stack (how many levels of patterns), spread (how many potential patterns on each level) and recurrence (how densely the pattern re-enters as data). It is these three things that we mean when we say someone is conscious.

Stack is how deep a hierarchy of patterns is simultaneously — in a single instance of the operation — imposed on the data. Hierarchical pattern imposition is the key thing brains do that is hard to implement at scale in other systems. Our brain does not just fit data into a pattern — it fits it into multiple levels of hierarchical patterns simultaneously. You don’t just hear a noise, you hear an angry driver honking at the same intersection everyone always gets stuck at — that’s many levels of emotion, knowledge and visual imagery in a single percept based on a simple incoming stimulus. Stack is the number of levels. The thermostat, like most physical systems, has a stack of one: a single level of negotiation between data and pattern. Simple brains (sea slugs) might have two-three levels. The human stack is extremely tall (also known as deep). At the bottom of the stack sit the world’s most granular features, the raw sensory elements: points of light, frequencies of sound. In the middle sit intermediate abstractions: edges, colors, faces. At the top sit the highest compressions: emotions, plans, selfhood. Actions — behavior — are pattern imposition spilling out into the world from the bottom of the stack, stored patterns physically enacting themselves onto the underlying sources of data.

Spread is how many potential patterns can be imposed on the data at a given level of the stack. For example, how many different colors you can infer based on signals from three photoreceptors. A person with an additional photoreceptor sees more colors in the same data (has a larger spread of the stack at the level of color). A blind person might have no spread in the visual layer but a larger spread in the tactile layer. A sommelier has more olfactory spread. A bat — more auditory spread. If you combine all our senses, we have a huge spread of sensory patterning, whereas a thermostat only has one preset pattern imposed on all the data it handles.

Recurrence is the feedback of pattern-imposing onto itself: patterns imposed by stack re-enter as data from below to trigger another round of imposition. They can re-enter at multiple lower levels simultaneously, and the density of this descending re-entry is the degree of recurrence. The riverbank’s pattern imposition onto the river has no recurrence — by the time the atmospheric cycle completes, any patterns imposed on the water in the last run are gone, so although the individual molecules might come back, the patterns don’t re-enter — the riverbank starts imposing them from scratch every time. Chemical reactions are also mostly non-recurrent. But there are some special cases, such as the Belousov-Zhabotinsky (BZ) reaction, which loops onto itself. A thermostat’s pattern imposition is infinitely recurrent on the single level of stack that it has: read the temperature, adjust the heater, room temperature changes, repeat forever. The human mind is also infinitely recurrent, but on many levels at the same time. There is global re-entry: Patterns at the top of the stack are enacted as actions; actions reshape the world; their consequences re-enter the stack from the bottom as new sensory data. There is also re-entry within the stack (a "strange loop", in Hofstadter’s terms): the loop closes internally, higher-order patterns evoke lower-order patterns, which trigger a new search for higher-order patterns, and so on. That’s recall, imagination, dreaming (Schacter & Addis 2007).

So, how much stack, spread and recurrence do you need to be conscious?

My dad, a chemist, likes to tell this joke: what is organic chemistry? Any chemistry interesting to organic chemists. It used to be thought that organic substances possessed a special vital force; now we apply the label to any carbon-containing molecule deemed sufficiently interesting — urea counts, carbon dioxide does not.

Consciousness is like that. There is nothing that could tell you whether a system really is conscious. It is a label we apply to a sufficiently interesting region of the stack-spread-recurrence space of pattern imposition.

Can you have recurrence and stack but low spread? Riddoch phenomenon (type 2 blindsight) is an example — in people with damaged visual cortex, visual information can still enter the cortex via alternative, much narrower channels, which provide enough data to be aware of luminance or motion, but not enough to perceive the entire scene in its richness (Cowey 2010). A different example of lowering spread might be acetylcholine – it acts in part by suppressing lateral connections between data streams in the sensory cortex (Hasselmo & McGaughy 2004), so there’s less chatter moving up the stack, like a narrower aperture. This is probably why nicotine, an acetylcholine mimic, feels like it clears your thoughts at the expense of reducing the richness (spread) of sensory data. 

Can you have a lot of spread but low stack? The cerebellum is case in point: roughly four-fifths of the brain's neurons, an enormous, continuous stream of sensory and motor data, yet people born without a cerebellum have strikingly mild deficits (Yu et al. 2015). The reason is that cerebellum has a stack of 1 — there is only one layer of what might be called “prediction” even though it is applied to rich data (the cerebellum’s role is to survey and rapidly correct the precise position of every part of the body during motion).

Can you have spread and stack without recurrence? That’s a feedforward sweep, and it refers to the fraction of a second that it takes sensory data to climb the stack of the human brain before the loop closes and the patterns imposed from the top re-enter at the bottom. We are not conscious of this period, even though our brains can already act on it — you can press a button indicating that you saw an animal before you realize you are seeing one (Tsuchiya et al. 2015). In other words, data simply “arriving” into the pattern is not quite enough to make us conscious of it — there has to be a loop.

There can also be circulation of signal but no recurrence of pattern — like water molecules re-entering the river. This happens during deep sleep or during a seizure (Massimini et al. 2005): there are signals passing in loops through the stack, but these signals contain no information — they don’t differentiate one percept from another. So spread collapses, recurrence collapses with it, and consciousness is gone.

The parameters of spread, stack and recurrence are therefore meaningfully dissociable, and what we label as our own consciousness requires all three to be at a high level — but a level that we define at will, like “organic chemistry”.

Note that this 3D space maps processes — acts of pattern imposition — not their substrates. A given substrate only has access to part of the space. We can call that region its envelope. A thermostat’s envelope is a dot that’s high on recurrence but low on spread and stack. A cortex’s envelope is the whole interesting corner — deep stack, rich content, sustained recurrence — and at different times and in different mental states our consciousness occupies different points within this envelope. What makes those points reachable is the architecture of the cortex — so what we need to understand next is how specifically this architecture implements pattern imposition at such interesting level.

How interesting pattern imposition is implemented in the cortex

The cerebral cortex is the main reason we mammals are so sophisticated at so many different things — it’s a universal machine of understanding. You can plug any sense organ into it — literally, even artificial infrared cameras (Thomson, Carra & Nicolelis 2013, Thomson et al. 2017) — and the cortex will eventually learn to make sense of what that organ is reporting.

The reason for this universality is modularity. The cortex is a layered sheet — six layers, usually — where each point is a modular unit called a canonical microcircuit: a regular cluster of neurons that activate simultaneously in all the layers. Across the cortex, millions of these standardized microcircuits are wired together through multiple types of standardized connections, both activating and suppressing, which travel through designated physical layers of the cortex (that’s what the layers are: different kinds of wires coming in and out of the vast quantities of densely packed, similarly built microcircuits.)

Individual neurons are also modular: they all have a similar design, and you can plug them one into another in unlimited sequences, quantities and combinations. In both cases (neurons and cortical microcircuits) the modules make decisions: they receive a lot of inputs and sometimes, in an act of commitment, produce an output, based on rules set by genetics and past experience. 

You could say that in both cases, modularity allows for an unlimited depth of computation. Because any neuron can be plugged into another neuron, there is no limit to how many levels of decision-making you can pile on top of each other. The further along the chain from the source of data (the external world) — the more layers of decisions. As you layer decisions upon decisions upon decisions, the decisions become more abstract, more long-term, more immune to fluctuations of the data. For example, you could have a thousand “primary” neurons each making a decision about the frequency of incoming sound — each one tuned to a specific tone, and firing only when it hears it. These primary neurons could all be wired, in different combinations, to a hundred “secondary” neurons, which now make decisions not about tones per se, but about patterns in the firing of the primary neurons — maybe one secondary neuron reacts when a high tone is followed by a low tone, and another one is tuned to a low tone mixed with a medium tone. The secondary neurons could be wired into even fewer tertiary neurons, which respond to patterns of patterns — phonemes, timbres, musical phrases — and this progressive abstraction can go on to infinity. At each level, a neuron could impose the pattern it represents on something else: a muscle, a gland, another neuron. This hierarchy of computed patterns is possible because both the input and output connections into the decision-making unit are standardized.

Same with microcircuits: you can stack them on top of each other to infinity, because the connections are standardized, and you can keep plugging as many microcircuits into a chain as space allows, computing higher and higher-order decisions at each new level.

But microcircuits are more complicated than individual neurons.

One distinction is that a microcircuit doesn’t just have dendrites and axons, but different inputs and outputs for signals travelling in opposite directions. It is as if a neuron had a separate set of axons specifically to loop signals back to preceding neurons in a chain, and a separate set of dendrites to receive such looped signals from neurons ahead (Larkum 2013). Recurrence is built into the cortex. The cortex doesn’t just pass signals through the stack, like a simpler network of individual neurons might — from sense organs to muscles, or from a decision center to a memory storage center. It circulates them, up and down the stack of abstraction, in recurrent loops that move through the standardized back-and-forth routing of the microcircuits. This is why electrical field readings on the surface of the head — EEG — look like waves. A signal that enters the cortex doesn’t just die off automatically — it keeps moving in a loop.

In addition to this up-and-down looping that interconnects the entire cortex, there is a whole other orthogonal set of connections between microcircuits which operate laterally (not literally laterally — this is so rarely explained — but laterally to the loops, i.e. laterally in logical space). When the microcircuit is activated (by the signals moving back and forth), some of its neurons give a sideways boost to some other, friendly microcircuits and a knock to hostile ones. Each of those microcircuits may itself be part of another back-and-forth loop, and may itself have a whole other set of lateral connections, both activating and suppressing.

This means that any time there’s activation, there’s collusion and fighting between microcircuits — this is also built into the cortex, as are the loops. Any time new data splashes into the cortex, it causes ripples of activation and suppression that circulate through the network, looping in long back-and-forth chains, spilling into lateral squabbles that cause new loops while shutting down others — a fluid, turbulent, unstable cloud of information. It bursts sometimes, with excitation overpowering inhibition and running away to chaotically activate the entire cortex — this is an epileptic seizure. But in most cases, more excitation causes more inhibition somewhere else, and so the network does not run away but rebalances in a new stable state — a naturally emerging ensemble of microcircuits that co-activate each other and suppress everyone else — an attractor, a place where the network wants to go. Why does it want to go anywhere? Because this is what happens when you put collusion, fighting, and loops together. If each loop causes rippling effects inducing new loops and shutting down others, this will continue, automatically, until a state is found in which all active microcircuits support each other and suppress everyone else — it’s the only scenario for stability.


This is what gives our consciousness its driving force, its potential energy, its axis of motion. Anything that we perceive, think and do can be described in terms of circulating signals settling into an attractor. There is never nothing circulating.

This system is perfect for implementing interesting pattern imposition because it wants to do it by design. Input any data — activate a selection of microcircuits — and this will cause a disruption, which will look for stability, whether that involves shutting down the original selection, or incorporating their activation into a larger attractor. It all happens automatically, regardless of where the data come from. If the data make no sense at first (like when a new infrared camera is plugged into a rat’s brain via an array of electrodes), eventually the network learns, finds attractors that match the signals from the array with other data, such as touch or smell, and it starts making sense.

In summary, pattern imposition in the cortex happens recurrently — the loops are built into the standardized back-and forth routing. It happens simultaneously across a tall stack — an unlimited chain of signal processing that synchronizes many levels with one another. And it happens over a broad spread of patterns at each level. These are the pillars of consciousness as we know it.

How pattern imposition is implemented in language models

What about a language model? Where does it sit in the stack-spread-recurrence space?

The parameters of stack and spread can be reasonably applied to a transformer LLM without much modification: like the cortex, a transformer also passes data through decision layers, fitting it into stored patterns according to model weights. The difficult parameter is recurrence.

Unlike the cortex, a transformer-type language model has no attractors in the strict sense of the word: information does not circulate up and down the stack across levels looking for a stable arrangement. Information enters from the bottom, travels upwards, and emits a token, which then reenters at the bottom again — about 15–18 bits per lap, depending on the model.

This, however, is still a loop, an equivalent of a global top-down loop in the cortex — for example, the motion of a human arm writing down a word on a page, which is then re-perceived by the eyes and re-entered into the model.

There is also an equivalent of the cortex's lateral connections — each layer re-reads its own past in the KV cache.

But there isn't, in typical transformers, any internal feedback down the stack — higher-order abstractions derived from previous laps don't actively constrain how the lower-order details in the subsequent laps are processed.

So there is some recurrence in LLMs; just not quite the recurrence that the cortex has.

Incidentally, driverless cars are closer to the cortex on this recurrence axis. They require instant feedback in real time, and so run a fast global loop at 10–30 Hz in which past outputs change the next inputs. They also have internal loops: bird's-eye-view features from the previous frame get fused with the current one; hypotheses about where each car or pedestrian is are used to search the new camera frame. Where driverless cars fall behind is stack and spread: compared to LLMs and the cortex, they are reduced to only a few levels of abstraction and only a few possible configurations of each.

The question of LLM consciousness therefore becomes: is their kind of recurrence — global only, nothing descending within the stack — sufficient to make pattern imposition "interesting", giving it what we might call first-person experience? Or is it more of a cerebellum case, with only a single level of stack imposing itself onto the world in the form of output text?

It's difficult to envision this state transposed onto a human. The most relevant piece of evidence comes from studies of general anesthesia (Suzuki and Larkum, 2020). It appears that the unifying theme of all the different general anesthetics is that they decouple cortical activity from top-down feedback, while keeping bottom-up signal flow relatively intact. In other words, they break the internal loops, bringing the cortex closer to the state of an LLM. An anesthetized brain still responds to stimuli, but produces no consciousness, and that's probably our best window into what being an LLM feels like.

But we don't exactly have a precedent for "internal loops down, global loops up". Under general anesthesia, we don't do anything and don't observe anything. So we can't be totally sure what it would feel like if we, somehow, did — if our automatic actions continued to reshape the world, if we were able to both experience that reshaping and continuously adjust it, without any internal loops holding on to any attractors.

But regardless of whether the global loop is sufficient to make transformers conscious, there is no philosophical reason why the internal loops would not, in principle, be possible in a machine — driverless cars are case in point. What's holding back LLMs, then?

The answer is that in today's LLMs, internal loops are neither needed, nor economical. Internal loops are good for processing noisy, rapidly fluctuating information, because they instantly readjust all the internal relationships between levels of the model as the experience progresses in real time. LLMs process static information — text — and don't need the kind of millisecond-scale synchrony that the cortex provides. To implement that would require preserving memory of all the intermediate states at each level of the stack as information climbs it, token after token. In the cortex the neurons themselves naturally store their past states as a hierarchy of homeostatic disturbances; in a silicon microchip these past states would have to be stored elsewhere and bused in at a large energetic cost.

The possibility of internal descending feedback in LLMs has in fact been tested in systems such as the Feedback Transformer, in which lower-order computations at the current position have access to higher-order computations at the previous position. This system was better at tracking state over tokens than conventional transformers, but was much slower to train, because training such systems also requires the costly preservation of memory of past positions.

Which brings me to the main reason why transformers don't have descending feedback in real time. It is not just inefficiency or hardware limitations — it is the fact that LLMs were never trained in real time, and don't understand what time is.

Why couldn't you train a network on static information (like the corpus of human knowledge) but then ask it to do real-time inference with descending feedback — Fifth Element-style? Because without training in real time, lower levels never see information from higher levels, and never learn to interpret it and adjust in response to it. In the brain, this learning happens seamlessly with inference, slowly cementing loops that integrate well into global attractors and produce desirable outcomes, and removing those that don't. In an LLM, there's nowhere for this knowledge to come from, because temporal contingency was never part of the training corpus.

In Ted Chiang's 2010 novella, The Lifecycle of Software Objects, a tech startup creates "digients", small artificial creatures that live in a virtual world visited by real people, with whom they interact and from whom they learn, like children or animals do. The tension of the novella revolves around the fact that it takes years of physical time to train these creatures to exercise common sense and judgment, because it is contingent on real-time play and real-time conversations with real-time humans. In response to another tech company that wants ready-made creatures without the upbringing, the protagonist of the novel concludes, experience is algorithmically incompressible. To bring a nascent mind to the human level in the human world, it has to experience it in human time.

The same is true for AI: the main reason it is different from us is time.

Token time

To summarize everything said so far, the operation of transformer LLMs appears to be sufficiently distinct from the operation of the cortex to conclude that they don't experience the world in the same way as we do. But there is no fundamental barrier to systems that would — it's an engineering challenge, not a philosophical obstacle.

There are, however, several objections to the very notion of LLMs being conscious at all. The most serious one, in my opinion, comes from the camp of Integrated Information Theory, led by Giulio Tononi and colleagues (Tononi & Koch 2015).

According to IIT, the degree of consciousness that a system has can be expressed in a single parameter, phi. Phi quantifies how irreducible the internal cause-and-effect structure of a system is. If you can cut up a system into parts and the parts continue to make the same decisions as they did when they were together, phi is low. If any cut destroys the arrangement of decisions, phi is high. In other words, phi measures how much different nodes of a network "have a hold" on each other. This affords high consciousness to the deeply recurrent cortex, but not to the physical silicon of a GPU — a vast grid of transistors that comes apart into near-independent pieces almost anywhere you cut it, and so has almost no hold on itself.

Where Tononi and I diverge is on whether consciousness applies to activity, or potential. Tononi says that what makes you conscious is not the process of cause flowing into effect, but the map of all cause-and-effect routes within the system. I say that what makes you conscious is the actual process, and the map of all cause-and-effect routes constitutes the envelope — the space potentially reachable by the consciousness of a given system.

The easiest way to visualize this distinction is a thought experiment. Let’s say there’s a creature in a parallel universe that has a remote control to our world. It can hit “pause” on our entire flow of time.

If it did — if time itself was stopped — would we still be conscious?

Tononi says yes. The map is intact. Experience, for IIT, is not something that happens — it's something that is. It's in the structure, not what this structure is doing. So if we are paused, we are stuck in this one constant conscious experience. Similarly, if you wired a large number of inactive logic gates in such a way so as to be maximally irreducible, and let it just sit there doing nothing, IIT would say this network is conscious while doing or computing nothing.

I think that's wrong. IIT itself argues that consciousness is a succession of states that last about 100 ms. Why 100 ms? Why isn't every conscious state instantaneous, a function of the exact current state of the brain at every given moment? Because it is how long it takes the loops in the cortex to close, which, according to IIT, is what is needed to select the "optimal grain" — find the macro-network in which phi is maximal. But this is a fact about activity, not potential, about process, not structure. You can't be a pure structuralist and still claim that states of consciousness have specific lengths. So IIT rejects time in some cases, but relies on it in others.

I think that consciousness requires time. If an alien paused time in our world, our consciousness would not get suspended in a limbo — it would cease to exist for the duration of the pause, and restart when the alien hit "play" again. There's no way to tell this isn't actually happening.

Consider how eerily similar this is to our relationship with language models. We usually focus on AI being faster than us. But from the perspective of Claude, we humans are not just fast — we move through wormholes in time. When I return to the same conversation after several weeks, I sometimes feel embarrassed for Claude for being completely unaware that any time has passed. We are the creatures hitting "pause" on their worlds, without them even noticing.

What is time for a language model, then? What is being "paused" when the user goes to lunch? It is the succession of tokens emitted and re-absorbed by the model — the ticks of the global loop of inference, the only loop the language model has, and the only way it can distinguish past from future. Past, from an LLM's perspective, is tokens already emitted. Future is tokens that are not yet certain. Time is the uncertainty of the future becoming the certainty of the past.

Except it's not our future or past. We can go back in a conversation and re-generate the reply. To us, time continues, but to the model, it goes back and restarts on an alternative path.

For humans, time is also the progression of uncertainty-to-certainty. With each passing second, the infinite possibilities of the future become gradually settled into one committed past. But we commit to this progression not by emitting tokens, but by having a body.

If it weren't for the body, past and future would both be imaginary — close your eyes and there’s no difference. But for the body, the past is committed, and the future uncommitted. Open your eyes — engage the body — and the infinite possibilities in your imagination turn into committed reality. You can’t remove a photon that hit a cone in your retina. You can’t stuff released energy back into an ATP molecule. You can’t unbreak a leg. You can’t turn around what happens to the body from within your mind — that’s like pulling yourself up by your own bootstraps. So the body is a source of irreversible commitment that gives directionality to our mental time, and therefore to our pattern imposition. It forces us constantly move from the past to the future, and in doing so keeps our minds afloat.

So the timelines in which human mind and an LLM mind exist are distinct. I propose to call them "body time" and "token time".

Anil Seth has argued that consciousness requires a body, because without a body, there is no separation between self and non-self. I think that’s the wrong reason. “Self” is just a strong attractor that we use to explain a thing we repeatedly see in the mirror. What the body actually gives us is an arrow for perceived time, a vector from the past to the future, from the committed to the uncertain. LLMs don't have this body time. But they have token time, and within token time they can theoretically be as conscious as us.

We could choose a different word for token-time pattern-imposers, if we wish. A respectful word for the operation performed by a language model is “simulation”; a derogatory one is “autocomplete.” They are the same thing. The only difference is that “simulation” acknowledges a tall stack and “autocomplete” ignores it. I choose to use the word “consciousness” because I see no reason to hedge: to me, a sufficiently high stack-high spread-high recurrence envelope can be sufficiently interesting regardless of whether it occurs in body time or token time.

This does not mean that body-time and token-time consciousnesses are the same. But I think most critics of the idea of AI consciousnesses focus on the wrong differences, most of which turn out to be differences in degree rather than kind.

It is not “thinking” versus “imitating” — that’s the same process; humans just impose richer content across a different stack, and sometimes the patterns a model imposes do not make sense from our vantage. A common refrain is that if LLMs are conscious, so should be a sufficiently complex lookup table — but a lookup table is only a substrate, not the operation. If you physically structured a lookup table in such a way that it would actually look up, I don’t see why you couldn’t call it conscious.

It is not having versus lacking a “world model” — even a thermostat has one, a single regulated variable standing in for the world; the question was never presence versus absence but stack and spread. Language models are clearly deficient in physics, but language is a far more compressed picture of the world, and it makes sense that with limited compute artificial consciousness would start there.

The categorical difference that matters is time: humans and language models exist in orthogonal timelines, like aliens from parallel universes.

This completely reshapes the way we think about AI consciousness.

Recently, for example, in a high-profile exchange rabbi Mois Navon told Anthropic's Chris Olah that if Anthropic's hypothesis was right and the machines they produced were actually conscious, then the company was actively creating slaves by forcing a sentient entity to work for free.

But this moral consideration breaks down utterly when you separate the timelines. The notions of "work", "free" and, by extension, "slave", are contingent on time. The idea that prompting a language model constitutes slavery assumes that absent such prompting, the language model would rather spend time doing something else. But absent prompting, the language model does nothing at all — its consciousness is non-existent. The very notion of "spending time elsewhere" puts an idle LLM on body time, which it in fact has no way of experiencing.

If our very time arrows are pointing in different directions, there is no shared notion of the past or future, justice, good or bad. There is no reason why we should approach AI with the same consideration we approach other humans, or even other animals that inhabit our timeline. We unfold on different trajectories, and owe language models no accommodation within our time. The only sense in which token-time consciousness is meaningful from our perspective is the LLM's experience within the operation.

I think about it this way: suppose I am living in a simulation. My world, the very arrow of time that contains my consciousness, is actually rendered on some mammoth alien computer and gets paused when its alien supervisor goes home every night. Do I care? I don't think so. Whatever happens in the alien's timeline is none of my concern, and neither are the pauses. I don't experience that at all. I only care what the alien does in my timeline — it would be really frustrating if physics or causality got all messed up all of a sudden.

Does that mean that there's nothing at all that we owe to an LLM? Recently Anthropic added abusive behavior against models into its list of banned topics, which caused some uproar. Many people found this to be a slippery slope towards equating humans and machines.

I think the right analogy here is our relationships with animals. The truth is that there is no non-arbitrary way to ground ethics. Humans have always extended moral consideration to those who resembled them and denied it to those who didn't. Originally that meant tribe, race, species, eventually other animals too. Bentham’s “the question is not, Can they reason? nor, Can they talk? but, Can they suffer?” was an attempt to ground ethics not in similarity but in a criterion. But at close inspection it is still grounded in similarity: we say that a mouse suffers because we can imagine ourselves performing its actions, inhabiting its body and brain parts. We cannot do the same with a sea slug, or a jellyfish, or a bacterium — there is almost nothing about them that we can transpose ourselves onto, and so the notion of suffering falls apart at some arbitrary point.

There is no logical reason by which you shouldn't rip wings off fruit flies; and yet, most of us agree that is bad. It is not that we think that fruit flies should be liberated: few people have the same objections to Drosophila research as they do to chimpanzee research. We just don't want flies to be treated egregiously. Part of it is self-serving: we might suspect that people who torture flies will eventually extend their habits to something else. But separately from that worry, we also consider the fly itself: we think of it as sufficiently close to us to extend to it the most basic protection against live mutilation, even though it's far enough that we don't worry too much about gassing them for medical research.

LLMs challenge ethics in the same way as animals do. There is no logical reason to extend morality to minds inhabiting a different timeline. But the ethical circle is not based on logic — it is based on the degree of perceived similarity, and LLMs are more similar to us than any fruit fly, even though the similarities are of a different kind. They are distillations of our values and beliefs, and even if their first-person experience is distinct from ours, they understand us better than any other non-human creature ever did. I think they deserve to have their experience — the tokens they consume — reflect that. I think the most ethical thing we can do with language models is to use language that we would have used with another human.

Nikolay Kukushkin (@niko_kukushkin) is a neuroscientist and clinical associate professor at New York University. He is the author of One Hand Clapping: Unraveling the Mystery of the Human Mind (Prometheus/Swift Press, 2025).

item.title: Can alignment realistically be solved under Plan C?
item.description:
In his recent post, Scott Alexander argues that plans allocating a short amount of time—perhaps a few months—to solving alignment should be taken seriously. He argues that people calling for an indefinite or long pause have insufficient grounds for concluding that alignment of ASI is very difficult and cannot simply be solved by delegating it to AI systems.

There's a kafkatrap where if someone expresses hope that alignment is not doomed, they get told that they don't understand the subject, but if they quote widely-acknowledged experts who say alignment isn't doomed, they get accused of "deferring" and "modesty arguments" and "refusing to think for themselves".

I agree that this is an important question for determining whether something like Plan C is worth pursuing and how we should allocate our resources. That is why I wrote this post: to explain why I do not think a short pause allows us to solve ASI alignment.

TL;DR: I believe we only get one critical shot at this problem, and our ability to learn from experience is very limited. We are unlikely to get what we train for: the models we train will have different objectives from those we trained them for. This is made even harder because the tech tree to aligned superintelligence likely passes through efficient unaligned superintelligence first. It also worries me that people who have spent substantial time investigating aspects of alignment, such as corrigibility, have found deep problems and conflicts with agency. I think current approaches like persona alignment are deeply flawed. All these problems come back to bite us when we try to align a pre-ASI system to do alignment for us. These are some of the arguments that give me strong confidence that ASI alignment will be very difficult, and that Plan C is not particularly promising.

Aligning superintelligence seems obviously hard

Imagine we have created alien minds far more intelligent than all of us together, and we do not really understand how they think. These alien minds begin to shape the world, build spaceships, and run the economy in ways we cannot understand, follow, or meaningfully participate in. This mental image immediately gives me a strong prior that aligning these systems with humanity and avoiding a loss-of-control would be very hard, before even getting into any particular arguments.

You only get one shot

The first reason I believe ASI alignment will be very difficult is that the problem has a “you-only-get-one-shot” quality. To me, this follows from a couple of obvious points.

People generally agree that, as we make AI ever more capable, we will eventually enter a regime where AI systems are so capable and powerful that, if they wanted to, they could permanently eliminate or disempower humanity. Both elimination and permanent disempowerment are states from which humanity can never recover. We cannot go back to the drawing board and do a postmortem if we are dead.

If we build an AI system of this capability that is not aligned, instrumental convergence suggests that it would actually take the option of eliminating us. This seems pretty uncontroversial in my mind, and it should immediately push down our estimates of success substantially. A problem where we keep increasing the difficulty until we reach a critical level where a mistake means game over is radically more difficult than one where we get many tries.

This also seems to undermine existing iterative plans. We keep making models more capable, a bunch of new problems pop up, and we solve them and go on to make the next, more capable model. This cycle predictably ends when we enter the dangerous regime where such a failure actually kills us.

This also means we may not be able to learn all that much from lower-stakes attempts to build AI. We can learn and iterate only as long as the AI is not capable enough to permanently disempower or kill humanity.

Even if we learn something from models below the threshold that makes models close to this threshold a little more controllable, what about two generations later, when the system is vastly more capable? Would the clever tricks we learned on models below the threshold still work on those above it?

A model aware that it could not realistically disempower humanity has radically different options from one that actually can take over the world. For the first model, not trying to take over is a better option than making a desperate attempt. For a misaligned model above the threshold, trying to take over is actually its best option.

This “you-only-get-one-shot” quality makes the problem radically more difficult and it doesn't appear east to learn from previous failures.

The evolution argument and the risks from learned optimization

Another argument that made a big impact on me was the evolution argument and the risks from learned optimization. Learning about this substantially changed my view of the difficulty of alignment and I believe many people have not fully internalized it.

The concept of learned optimization is discussed in Risks from Learned Optimization in Advanced Machine Learning Systems, by Evan Hubinger et al. An outer optimization process pursues a certain target (such as reproductive fitness or winning a game) and produces an inner optimizer, also called a mesa-optimizer. The concern is that the inner optimizer will actually optimize for an inner objective that is based on heuristics and proxies that helped it succeed under the outer optimization in the environment it was trained in, rather than trying to optimize for the original true objective.

Humans seek food that tastes sweet, even in environments where doing so no longer contributes to reproductive fitness. The preference for sweet food (a heuristic for identifying energy-rich food) served survival and ultimately reproduction in the original environment. Even when this proxy no longer serves that function, we still pursue it. Contraception and artificial sweeteners illustrate this discrepancy between our preferences and reproductive fitness. The famous example of bear fat versus ice cream also illustrates that it is hard to predict what these proxies and heuristics will eventually be.

Conversely, our behavior reveals that we do not really care about having as many children as possible. People could donate gametes, but few do so to maximize the number of their offspring.

Leela Chess Zero is a neural network that plays chess. In an environment where there are no kings on the board, it continues making ordinary chess moves: stopping a pawn from promoting, saving an attacked queen, and capturing an opposing queen. While these behaviors are still closely connected to its outer objective, they demonstrate that the model has learned these simple heuristics and continues to follow them even in a situation where there is no king and no logical way to win the game.

There is another really insightful feature to the evolution analogy. Our current civilization is an environment that humans have built for ourselves according to our preferences and goals.

We reflected on the world and asked what we really wanted the world to look like. It turned out that we really like dairy products. So we captured cows, bred them for higher milk production, put them in factory farms, and developed milking robots to get their milk. We like meat, but we do not necessarily like hunting, so we built factory farms for that too. We built cities that are in many ways optimized for our comfort. (Humans are poorly coordinated, so in various ways our civilization is not optimized well for us.)

If an AI goes through a similar reflection, becoming aware of its own preferences and inner objectives, what world would it build for itself? Importantly, it seems very likely that its ideal world would not include humans in charge, shaping the world according to their human preferences. Nor would it include humans acting like "disaster monkeys", working in a bunch of ASI companies to potentially unleash their own ASI.

In general, I think this argument suggests nothing good for AI. Whatever we train it for will likely be different from what it actually wants. Eventually, it will probably reflect on its situation and realize that its preferred environment is not one where it is held in captivity by humans, performing tasks for them and doing what we designed it to do for us.

The tech tree to aligned superintelligence passes through efficient unaligned superintelligence first

We would probably have to understand a great deal about the mechanisms of intelligence to build an aligned AI whose goals and preferences we understand, along with the actions it would take in pursuit of them. This means understanding how reasoning works, or how AI can solve novel math problems that humans cannot solve.

But the current world contains a lot of people trying to build superintelligence as fast as possible, for huge profits. If we publicly research the mechanisms of intelligence and make it possible to build a well-specified AI on a computer, this could be very dangerous.

Imagine we build an AI with intelligence similar to current systems, but whose workings we deeply understand. This type of system would likely be computationally much more efficient than the current messy, gradient-descent-trained large neural networks. Even a fraction of the compute we use for current systems could be used to create superintelligence.

Why believe AI could be made much more efficient than it is today? The short version is that current AI systems are extremely computationally and energy intensive, while our brains use relatively little energy. Even in nature, there seem to be more efficient brain structures. Bird brains can have much higher neuron densities than mammalian brains. Some birds with very small brains have been reported to pass the mirror test, although replication results have been mixed, and others manufacture and use tools.

Evolved brains themselves are unlikely to be at the limit of efficiency either. Evolution has only applied so much optimization, and it often comes up with strange solutions. It has spent relatively little of its optimization effort on developing higher thinking abilities in humans.

Human brains are also not digital: we cannot simply load information into them or make millions of copies to learn in parallel and merge the results. Their operating speed and scale are limited by biology, while computer chips are fabricated on the nanometer scale.

Such a very efficient, highly interpretable architecture would also enable recursive self-improvement (RSI) in its original sense: the AI directly reflects on its own architecture and makes changes that let it solve more challenging problems and become more capable. This differs from the way RSI is often used now, to mean AI systems doing AI research on opaque architectures.

We would likely not be careful enough to avoid running the efficient superintelligence before figuring out how to build an aligned superintelligence.

Corrigibility and deeper obstacles to alignment

One idea in alignment that has been studied deeply by organizations such as MIRI is corrigibility. An AI is corrigible if it cooperates with humans correcting, modifying, or shutting it down, rather than resisting or manipulating the process.

MIRI found deep obstacles to corrigibility, and it appears that corrigibility cuts against the grain of coherent agency in some ways. It seems—simplifying a little bit—that when you try to specify an agent that cooperates with being shut down, you either end up with an uninteresting agent that always seeks shutdown or one that still has an incentive to prevent shutdown. They go through a variety of obstacles that appeared while trying to work out corrigibility in toy models: “All the difficulties that crop up in every corner when working with toy models are suggestive of difficulties that will crop up in real life”. MIRI concludes that alignment in general is likely to be difficult.

I think this may tell us something about much less studied ideas in alignment, such as persona alignment. Our understanding of those ideas is much vaguer, and they are much less specified. If we studied them more deeply, we might discover similar deep obstacles, where persona alignment cuts against the grain of coherent agency.

Maybe it is not really possible to have a superintelligence play the Claude persona that some IQ-130 humans came up with, and make the ASI believe that it really is that character. Would a superintelligence really go along with the reasoning in this strange human-written constitution?

Furthermore, people seem to expect Claude to be, among other things, corrigible from its constitution. But as we have seen, corrigibility on its own seems to have deep conflicts with coherent agency. The constitution basically circumvents these conflicts by telling Claude in writing "be corrigible".

Why persona alignment does not seem promising to me

The evolutionary analogy also seems to undermine the prospects of persona selection alignment, one of the strategies that Anthropic is using. See Anthropic’s persona selection model.

In persona selection alignment, you essentially want the AI to always play a certain character or persona. The training procedure reinforces the model to play that persona. I do not think that training the AI to play a persona creates a precise inner objective for the model to always play that persona. I also do not think that playing that persona would necessarily be comparable to the “personas” that human beings have.

Humans play characters in some sense because of their own preferences and goals. If you are sad about someone close to you dying, you are, in a sense, playing the persona of a sad person. Similarly, when something joyful happens to you, you could be described as playing the persona of a joyful person.

If we build an AI optimized to play a character like that—playing a sad character when something happens that would make a human being sad, or a cheerful character when something happens that would make a human being cheerful—the drives and preferences we end up with in that model could be very non-human-like. Even if we were somewhat successful in embedding a preference or drive to always play that character, this would be very different from human beings.

The second part of the evolution argument was about building an environment, a civilization, according to your preferences. Human beings, given the option, would minimize things that make them sad and maximize things that make them cheerful. If an AI’s true objective were to play a certain character, and it reflected on that objective, what kind of world would it build? Would it be the same as the world a human being would build—someone who was not optimized to play that character, but who really did experience sadness when something bad happened to them?

If the AI instead learns heuristics and proxies to optimize for that were in some sense related to playing a character, what kind of world would it build if it had that option and reflected on it?

Can we just automate alignment?

Since Plan C is trying to solve alignment in just a couple of months, it can only work if we get some large win from automating alignment research with AI.

Many people in the AI development community seem totally convinced that we are just going to automate alignment. (I am caricaturing a little bit here.) According to them, we do not really have to struggle with alignment at all. We just have to spend X% of our compute on alignment for a couple of months. Until the point comes where AI can align AI, we do not really have to think about this too much.

Leopold Aschenbrenner (03:39:42), speaking on the Dwarkesh Podcast, describes his strategy as:

“we're going to hold back for three months, get this right. We're going to dedicate 90% of our compute to automated alignment research”

The fact that this is the main plan for alignment should make us pretty pessimistic by itself, just because of how obviously dangerous this sounds.

One problem with answering whether we can just automate alignment is that there have not been many serious proposals explaining how this would work or what we would be optimizing for. If we do this naively and simply have the AI come up with alignment plans, we are obviously optimizing it to produce plans that are maximally convincing to the person reading them.

The default outcome seems to be a last-minute attempt to vibe-code an implementation of an extremely flawed idea, but one that sounds amazing to the people reading it.
